## Preprocessing

Lines are read verbatim and normalised to a single Unicode form. Nothing is
lowercased, filtered or reordered. Both `NFC` and `NFD` variants are built and
carried through the ablation sweep.

## What this corpus cannot tell you

This corpus is professionally translated news and encyclopaedic prose, and its
limits follow from that.

**Domain.** It contains no assistant chat register, no code, no
transliterated or Latin-script Indic, and no user-generated text. Real Indian
traffic is heavily code-switched and frequently Latin-script; none of it is
represented here, so no number in this submission forecasts production token
cost. It measures how a tokenizer handles clean edited prose.

**Translationese.** Every sentence is a translation of a shared English source,
so Indic phrasing is pulled toward English structure. Word order, clause length
and lexical choice are all more English-like than natural Indic text would be.
If that biases the fertility ratios, it biases them *downward* — natural text
would likely diverge further, not less.

**Sample size.** 1012 parallel sentences give intervals tight enough
to separate the tokenizers and denominators compared here, and that is all they
give. They say nothing about tails, and capacity planning fails on tails rather
than means: the ninety-ninth-percentile long request decides whether a server
preempts, and one thousand sentences of uniform news prose cannot describe it.

**Parallelism is an artefact of construction.** The per-sentence denominator is
meaningful precisely because index *i* is the same proposition in every
language — a property this corpus has by design and real traffic never has. The
comparison is therefore valid as a controlled measurement and is not a
simulation of production.
